html:
Secret rites held each year at Eleusis, near Athens, for the goddesses Demeter and Persephone. Initiates were promised a happier fate after death. The cult probably began well before the 6th century BCE, when it was already under Athens.

The myth behind it told how Hades carried off Persephone, how Demeter's grief made the earth barren, and how Persephone returned each spring. In the autumn, crowds walked the Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis. What happened inside the hall of initiation was never to be told, and the secret was largely kept for a thousand years. Initiates drank a barley drink called kykeon.

The Mysteries were open to men and women, free and slave, as long as they spoke Greek and had not shed blood. Aeschylus was born in Eleusis, and Alcibiades was charged in 415 BCE with mocking the rites. Romans, including emperors, were initiated too. The cult ended when Theodosius I closed the pagan sanctuaries in the 390s CE.
